Do Now: Pixel Lab Recap

Quick recap from last lesson before today's sound challenges start.

items.prompt: Increasing the colour depth of an image mainly gives you...
options: A smaller file, with fewer colours
A larger file, with more possible colours
A larger image, with the same colours
items.explain: More bits per pixel means more possible colour values (2^depth), at the cost of a larger file.

items.prompt: Image resolution is best described as...
options: The number of colours an image can use
The number of pixels used to make up the image
How compressed the image file is
items.explain: Resolution is the number of pixels (width x height) used to represent the image - not colours, not compression.

steps.label: Sound Lab
steps.content:
Data Representation

Sound Lab

Year 10, 1.2 L3 · Sound · 30 minutes

  • Concept: How a computer turns a continuous sound wave into stored numbers.
  • Challenge 1: Drag the sample rate and watch (and hear) the recording fall apart.
  • Challenge 2: Do the same with sample resolution.
  • Challenge 3: Free play with both, and listen to the difference for yourself.
  • Real world: Compare CD audio, phone calls and voice memos.

steps.label: What Is Sound, Digitally?
steps.content:
What Is Sound, Digitally?

A real sound - your voice, a guitar string, a car horn - is a continuous wave: air pressure changing smoothly, with no gaps and no fixed steps. A computer can only store numbers, so it has to turn that smooth wave into a list of them.

It does this by sampling: measuring the height of the wave at regular instants in time, then rounding each measurement to the nearest value it can actually store. Two settings control how faithful that recording is:

  • Sample rate - how many measurements are taken per second. Too few, and fast changes in the wave get missed entirely.
  • Sample resolution - how many bits are used to store each measurement. Too few, and every measurement gets rounded to a nearby value that is only roughly right.

Both of these work exactly like resolution and colour depth did for images last lesson - more of either means a more faithful copy of the original, and a bigger file.

steps.label: Exam Question: Name the Term
steps.content:
Exam Question: Name the Term

A real Cambridge exam question (0478/13, June 2025, Question 1) asked students to complete a table about converting sound to binary.

items.prompt: Which term means "the measurement of the height (amplitude) of a sound wave taken at regular time intervals"?
options: A sample
The sample rate
The sample resolution
The bit depth
items.explain: Each single measurement of the wave is a sample. The rate is how often they are taken; the resolution is how many bits store each one.

steps.label: Challenge 3: Free Play and Listen
steps.content:
Challenge 3: Free Play and Listen

Both sliders are unlocked. File size in bits/sec = sample rate × sample resolution. Try to find the lowest settings where the tone is still clearly recognisable - then press Play to check by ear, not just by eye.

steps.label: Real-World Sample Rates
steps.content:
Real-World Sample Rates

The same trade-off you just explored decides the settings real recording formats actually use:

FormatSample rateSample resolutionWhy
Telephone call8,000 Hz8-bitSpeech is still understandable at low quality, and it keeps the amount of data sent very small.
Voice memo / podcast44,100 Hz16-bitClear speech and music without an enormous file.
CD audio44,100 Hz16-bitThe standard for near-transparent music quality.
Studio recording96,000 Hz24-bitExtra headroom for editing and mixing before the final release.

Notice a phone call uses a much lower sample rate than music - a smaller file matters more than perfect quality when speech only needs to be understood, not enjoyed.

Adapted from the same real exam question. A student records a song; two bytes stored from the recording are 00011001 and 10110100. A third value, the two’s complement 8-bit integer 11001001, is also stored.

steps.label: Practice: Sample Rate in Context
steps.content: Practice: Sample Rate in Context

items.prompt: What is one effect of increasing the sample rate of a recording?
options: The recording follows the original wave more closely, and the file gets larger
The recording uses fewer bits per sample
The recording becomes shorter
The number of amplitude levels goes down
items.explain: More samples per second capture fast changes in the wave that a lower rate would miss - at the cost of more data.

items.prompt: Why does a telephone call use a lower sample rate than a music recording?
options: Speech only needs to be understood, so a smaller file and less data to send matters more than high quality
Phone lines cannot carry high sample rates at all
A lower sample rate makes voices sound clearer
Music files are always stored uncompressed
items.explain: A phone call trades quality for a much smaller amount of data to transmit, because intelligible speech does not need the detail music does.

steps.label: Plenary: Sound
steps.content:
Plenary: Sound

Answer from memory - no notes, no going back to the challenges.

items.prompt: What is meant by the sample rate of a sound recording?
options: The number of samples (measurements) taken per second
The number of bits used to store each sample
The length of the recording in seconds
The loudness of the recording
items.explain: Sample rate is measured in samples per second (Hz).

items.prompt: What is meant by the sample resolution of a sound recording?
options: The number of bits used to store each sample
The number of samples taken per second
The number of seconds the recording lasts
The number of audio channels
items.explain: Sample resolution (bit depth) is bits per sample - it fixes how many different amplitude values can be recorded.

items.prompt: Sample resolution is increased. What happens to the recording and the file?
options: Each measurement is more precise, and the file gets larger
Each measurement is less precise, and the file gets smaller
The recording plays faster
Only the sample rate is affected
items.explain: More bits per sample means finer amplitude steps (a more faithful copy) and more data stored.

items.prompt: Calculate the number of bits needed to store 2 seconds of sound sampled at 10 samples/sec with a 4-bit sample resolution.
options: 80 bits
40 bits
160 bits
20 bits
items.explain: 10 samples/sec x 4 bits = 40 bits per second, and 40 x 2 seconds = 80 bits.

y10_1_2_l3_exambinary.feedback: Add up the place values for each 1 - the same method you used in 1.1.
Same method as before - add up the place values for each 1 in this byte.
Split the byte into its two nibbles and convert each nibble to hex separately.
The leading 1 means this is negative - invert the bits and add 1, the same as in 1.1, then remember the minus sign.

y10_1_2_l3_practice.feedback: Multiply the sample rate by the sample resolution.
Number of levels is 2 to the power of the bit depth.
Multiply the sample rate by the sample resolution.
